item.title: Hash Collisions: Why Your 'Unique' Fingerprints Aren't (And Why That's Usually OK)
item.description:
In 2017, Google researchers generated two different PDF files with identical SHA-1 hashes, finally proving what cryptographers had warned about for years: hash functions don’t create truly unique fingerprints. This “SHAttered” attack required 9 quintillion SHA-1 computations—equivalent to 6,500 years of single-CPU computation. The attack cost approximately $45,000 in cloud computing resources, making it accessible to well-funded adversaries but not casual attackers.

Yet despite this proof, we still trust hash functions for everything from Git commits to blockchain transactions to password storage. The reason is simple: while collisions are mathematically inevitable, meaningful collisions remain virtually impossible. The full story of hash collisions is more nuanced than “unique” versus “not unique.”

*“In cryptography, ‘secure’ has always meant ‘secure for now’.”
